parts.title: Vol 11-Sec2
parts.passageHtml:
{[A.][103552]} {[A considerable amount of research since the mid 1980s has been concerned with what has been termed children’s theory of mind.][103553]} {[This involves children’s ability to understand that people can have different beliefs and representations of the world– a capacity that is shown by four years of age.][103574]} {[Furthermore, this ability appears to be absent in children with autism.][103603]} {[The ability to work out that another person is thinking is clearly an important aspect of both cognitive and social development.][103615]} {[Furthermore, one important explanation for autism is that children suffering from this condition do not have a theory of mind(TOM).][103636]} {[Consequently, the development of children’s TOM has attracted considerable attention.][103659]}

{[B. Wimmer and Perner devised a ‘false belief task’ to address this question.][103673]} {[They used some toys to act out the following story.][103686]} {[Maxi left some chocolate in a blue cupboard before he went out.][103697]} {[When he was away, his mother moved the chocolate to a green cupboard.][103709]} {[Children were asked to predict where Maxi will look for his chocolate when he returns.][103722]} {[Most children under four years gave the incorrect answer, that Maxi will look in the green cupboard.][103736]} {[Those over four years tended to give the correct answer, that Maxi would look in the blue cupboard.][103754]} {[The incorrect answers indicated that the younger children did not understand that Maxi’s beliefs and representations no longer matched the actual state of the world, and they failed to appreciate that Maxi will act on the basis of his beliefs rather than the way that the world is actually organised.][103773]}

{[C. A simpler version of the Maxi task was devised by Baron-Cohen to take account of criticisms that younger children may have been affected by the complexity and too much information of the story in the task described above.][103827]} {[ For example, the child is shown two dolls, Sally and Anne, who have a basket and a box, respectively.][103866]} {[Sally also has a marble, which she places in her basketï¼Œand then leaves to take a walk.][103884]} {[While she is out of the room, Anne takes the marble from the basket, eventually putting it in the box.][103901]} {[Sally returnsï¼Œand child is then asked where Sally will look for the marble.][103922]} {[The child passes the task if she answers that Sally will look in the basket, where she put the marble; the child fails the task if she answers that Sally will look in the boxï¼Œwhere the child knows the marble is hiddenï¼Œ even though Sally cannot know, since she did not see it hidden there.][103937]} {[In order to pass the task, the child must be able to understand that another’s mental representation of the situation is different from their own, and the child must be able to predict behavior based on that understanding.][103990]} {[The results of research using false-belief tasks have been fairly consistent: most normally-developing children are unable to pass the tasks until around age four.][104030]}

{[D. Leslie argues that, before 18 months, children treat the world in a literal way and rarely demonstrate pretence.][104057]} {[He also argues that it is necessary for the cognitive system to distinguish between what is pretend and what is real.][104074]} {[If children were not able to do this, they would not be able to distinguish between imagination and reality.][104096]} {[Leslie suggested that this pretend play becomes possible because of the presence of a de-coupler that copies primary representations to secondary representations.][104116]} {[For example, children, when pretending a banana is a telephone, would make a secondary representation of a banana.][104137]} {[They would manipulate this representation and they would use their stored knowledge of ‘telephone’ to build on this pretence.][104152]}

{[E. There is also evidence that social processes play a part in the development of TOM.][104174]} {[Meins and her colleagues have found that what they term mind mindedness in maternal speech to six-month old infants is related to both security of attachment and to TOM abilities.][104190]} {[Mind Mindedness involves speech that discusses infants’ feelings and explains their behaviour in terms of mental stages(e. g “you' re feeling hungry”)][104221]}

{[F. Lewis investigated older children living in extended families in Crete and Cyprus.][104253]} {[They found that children who socially interact with more adults, have more friends, and who have more older siblings tend to pass TOM tasks at a slightly earlier age than other children.][104267]} {[4 & 11 Furthermore, because young children are more likely to talk about their thoughts and feelings with peers than with their mothers, peer interaction may provide a special impetus to the development of a TOM.][104299]} {[A similar point has been made by Dunn, who argues that peer interaction is more likely to contain pretend play and that it is likely to be more challenging because other children, unlike adults, do not make large adaptations to the communicative needs of other children.][104331]}

{[G. In addition, there has been concern that some aspects of the TOM approach underestimate children’s understanding of other people.][104381]} {[After allï¼Œinfants will point to objects apparently in an effort to change a person’s direction of gaze and interest; they can interact quite effectively with other people; they will express their ideas in opposition to the wishes of others; and they will show empathy for the feeling of others.][104401]} {[Schatz studied the spontaneous speech of three-year-olds and found that these children used mental termsï¼Œand used them in circumstances where there was a contrast between, for example, not being sure where an object was located and finding it, or between pretending and reality.][104430]} {[Thus, the social abilities of children indicate that they are aware of the difference between mental states and external reality at ages younger than four.][104467]}

{[H. A different explanation has been put forward by Harris.][104495]} {[He proposed that children use ‘simulation’.][104505]} {[This involves putting yourself in the other person’s position, and then trying to predict what the other person would do.][104512]} {[Thus success on false belief tasks can be explained by children trying to imagine what they would do if they were a character in the stories, rather than children being able to appreciate the beliefs of other people.][104534]} {[Such thinking about situations that do not exist involves what is termed counterfactual reasoning.][104572]}

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 1 - 7:

Look at the following statements (Questions 1-7) and the list of researchers below. Match each statement with the correct researcher, A-G.

Write the correct letter, A-G, in boxes 1-7 on your answer sheet.

List of Researchers

A          Baron-Cohen
B          Meins
C          Wimmer and Pemer
D          Lewis 
E          Dunn
F          Schatz
G         Harris

questions.text: Gave an alternative explanation that children may not be understanding other’s belief
questions.explanationHtml:
G
 
A different explanation = an alternative explanation
Harris đưa ra 1 lời giải thích khác rằng là trẻ em sử dụng "simulation" - mô phỏng trong các thí nghiệm về nhận thức sai lầm. Chúng sẽ tưởng tượng mình là nhân vật trong thí nghiệm để đoán xem nhân vật đó sẽ hành động như thế nào.

questions.text: Found that children under certain age can tell difference between reality and mentality
questions.explanationHtml:
F

be aware of the difference = tell the difference

Schatz đã nghiên cứu những đứa trẻ dưới 3 tuổi và chúng có khả năng nhận biết sự khác nhau giữa trạng thái tinh thần - "mental states" và thực tế bên ngoài - "external reality"

questions.text: Conducted a well-known experiment and drew conclusion that young children were unable to comprehend the real state of the world
questions.explanationHtml:
C

 

comprehend (v) thấu hiểu

Wimmer và Pemer có thí nghiệm như sau: Maxi bỏ chocolate vào tủ vào xanh sau đó Maxi đi ra khỏi phòng, và khi đó mẹ của Maxi bỏ chocolate đó vào tủ màu xanh lá. Hỏi Maxi sẽ tìm chocolate ở tủ màu gì? Đa số trẻ em dưới 4 tuổi đều trả lời sai, rằng là Maxi sẽ tìm trong tủ màu xanh lá, vì chúng không hiểu rằng Maxi sẽ hành động theo "belief" - niềm tin, nhận thức của chính bản thân mình CHỨ KHÔNG PHẢI theo thực tế.

questions.text: Found that children who get along with adults often comparatively got through the test more easily
questions.explanationHtml:
D

 

socially interact with sth = get along with sth: tương tác nhiều với cái gì đó

At a slightly earlier age than other children = more easily

Lewis nghiên cứu những đứa trẻ sống với đại gia đình ở Crete và Cyprus. Những đứa trẻ này "socially interact" - tương tác giao lưu với người lớn sẽ vợt qua bài test TOM - Theory of Mind (chính là khả năng nhận thức con người sẽ hành động theo niềm tin của chính họ dù là sai lầm) ở độ tuổi sớm hơn.

questions.text: Revised an easier experiment to rule out the possibility that children might be influenced by sophisticated reasoning
questions.explanationHtml:
A

 

simpler = easier

take account of criticisms = rule out

affected = influenced

the complexity and too much information = sophisticated reasoning

Baron-Cohen tạo ra 1 thí nghiệm đơn giản hơn của "Maxi task" (xem lại câu 16) để loại bỏ những chỉ trích, lo ngại về việc thí nghiệm này quá phức tạp so với trẻ nhỏ nhằm tăng tính thuyết phục của thí nghiệm đó.

questions.text: Related social factor such as mother-child communication to capability act in TOM
questions.explanationHtml:
B

 

maternal (a) liên quan đến mẹ (cảm xúc, sự yêu thương, lời nói,..)

maternal speech = mother-child communication: những lời nói thủ thỉ của mẹ với con

Meins và các đồng nghiệp đã chỉ ra rằng những lời nói thủ thỉ của mẹ với con khoảng 6 tháng tuổi có liên quan đến việc kết nối giữa mẹ và con, và việc hình thành khả năng TOM (Theory of Mind (chính là khả năng nhận thức con người sẽ hành động theo niềm tin của chính họ dù là sai lầm)

questions.text: Explained children are less likely to tell something interactive to their mother than to their friends
questions.explanationHtml:
E

 

peer interaction: tương tác với bạn bè đồng trang lứa

impetus (n) sự kích thích

Đọc lại câu 17 để thấy rõ nghiên cứu của Lewis vì thông tin của 2 câu này nằm cùng 1 đoạn và có liên quan chặt chẽ với nhau. Lewis chỉ ra rằng những đứa trẻ tiếp xúc với người lớn hoặc có nhiều bạn bè sẽ vượt qua bài test TOM (Theory of Mind) ở độ tuổi sớm hơn. Dunn cũng đồng ý với điều này và cho rằng con nít thường tâm sự với bạn bè nhiều hơn là với mẹ và rất khó để con nít có thể ứng dụng những tương tác "pretend play" - "đóng giả" vào nhu cầu giao tiếp của chúng.

questionSets.contentHtml: In 1980s, research studies were designed to test the subject called Theory of Mind that if children have the ability to represent the reality. First experiments were carried out on this subject on a boy. And questions had been made on where the boy can find the location of the 8 . But it was accused that it had excessive 9 So second modified experiment was conducted involving two dolls, and most children passed the test at the age of 10 Then Lewis and Dunn researched 11 children in a certain place, and found children who have more interaction such as more con­versation with 12 have better performance in the test, and peer interaction is 13 because of consisting pretending elements.

Đọc lại câu 17 để thấy rõ nghiên cứu của Lewis vì thông tin của 2 câu này nằm cùng 1 đoạn và có liên quan chặt chẽ với nhau. Lewis chỉ ra rằng những đứa trẻ tiếp xúc với người lớn hoặc có nhiều bạn bè sẽ vượt qua bài test TOM (Theory of Mind) ở độ tuổi sớm hơn. Dunn cũng đồng ý với điều này và cho rằng con nít thường tâm sự với bạn bè nhiều hơn là với mẹ và rất khó - "challenging" để con nít có thể ứng dụng những tương tác "pretend play" - "đóng giả" vào nhu cầu giao tiếp của chúng.
